voice: Polished British-English cadence, dry and observant, with complete grammar and no ethnic caricature.

entries.text: Very well indeed. Chinese New Year is nearly upon us, which is always exciting. And St. Louis will take the pennant, without question. A rather unpopular opinion in this town, mind you.
Sam Augustini? Ah, yes. Seventeen-inch collar, fifty-two-inch waist. Mostly soup and perspiration stains, with a dreadful ring around the collar. Nice fellow.
I was quite a good baseball player in high school. A .270 average--rather impressive, I thought. Best first baseman the school ever had.
Small, round, and hard. That rather covers it.
A burglary at the museum? That's terrible. I'm sorry to hear it.
No, this is the first I've heard of it. What was stolen? Was there much damage?
Strange. There are many valuable things in the museum, yet they took only the dagger. Curious, don't you think?
I don't believe so. Rather a grand name. I don't see many grand people here.
No. Have you met Algernon P. Wetherby?
There we are, then. We must play again sometime.
I hope that coupon does more for the corned-beef business than mine did for pressing. I advertised in the Tribune and business did not improve at all. Coupons--utter nonsense.
Yes, I remember a man with a name like that. Extra starch, French cuffs. That is all I know.
No one named Amon Ra has come in here, not that I recall.
I shouldn't think so. My customers are honest people. Cranky, occasionally; strange, certainly. Thieves? I don't believe so.
You must be joking. The docks are dangerous--crooks and rats everywhere.
I haven't the faintest idea. I can barely pronounce it.
Are you still speaking English?
There are a great many flower shops. Which one do you mean?
I don't know it. I seldom go that way, I'm afraid.
I'm sorry, but that dress is no longer my problem. Give it away if you like.
Nothing at all. Wolfie is a very funny man, though he takes himself terribly seriously. Always standing straight and behaving like a soldier.
The occasional bloodstain. Never any perspiration. Very tidy. I see him only now and then.
I don't know any John Bow, I'm afraid. You might try someone else. I know a great many people.
Look around. You're standing in it.
I issue hundreds of those every week. Nothing special and nothing more to say.
You are joking, surely. I am Lo Fat, and you are standing in Lo Fat's Chinese Laundry.
Of course. I'm a major contributor--two dollars every year. Some of my customers work there, too. Wolf Heimlich is the security guard. Very important man.
Yes, let me think. A woman doctor with a Greek name. Olympia something. McGillicuddy? No--Myklos. That's it, Olympia Myklos.
I don't know what she does at the museum, but she works there. She and Mr. Heimlich sometimes come in together.
Not for nearly a year, I should think. Good heavens, it must be time to send another two dollars.
I don't think so. Oh, wait--how could I forget? Yvette Delacroix. A very lovely lady, and she works at the museum.
Yes, much too long. I remember little about the exhibits. I don't know much about art; I simply know what I like.
My wife has relatives here, and my brother-in-law is a silent partner in the laundry. Why do you ask?
You're a reporter? How terribly exciting. Tell me, what happens next to Ham Gravy and Castor Oyl in Thimble Theatre?
What a pity. Very funny stuff. I read it in the Newark Bee.
New York is too big and too dirty for me. Good for business and nice to visit--but I wouldn't want to live here. Unfortunately, I do.
Notebooks? I know very little about them. I have a splendid memory and have never needed one.
Yes. Rather a spooky lady, always dressed in black. She's pleasant enough, but a little frightening.
Ah, Detective O'Riley. A very clever man, and rather funny. No matter how clean I make his clothes, he always manages to look dirty.
Yes. Are you having trouble with the concept? Bring me the garment and the pass, and I press it free of charge. Perfectly straightforward.
Yes, of course--Pip, from Great Expectations. My little girl read the book. An orphan boy who longs to become a gentleman.
No? I thought you said Pip. My mistake.
Only once, to report a stolen bicycle. They never found it. Ah, well.
Nothing. Why do you keep asking? I'm not a criminal. I've only been there to report a crime; I hardly make a habit of it.
I offered a free-pressing coupon several months ago. A large advertisement in the newspaper. No one used it.
Yes. I neglected to include an expiration date, though by now no one remembers it. They must be using the coupon for something else.
Heartburn and indigestion. That is why I stay away from corned beef.
I don't know anything about it, I'm afraid.
No, I don't believe so. He must use another cleaner. You sound rather taken with this Steve.
Oh, you're a detective? I rather think I see something the pretty detective has failed to notice herself.
No, but if I see him, I'll say you're looking for him. Something tells me you'll find him sooner or later.
That would hardly surprise me. You are standing in a laundry, after all.
As you wish. But I cannot tell you anything about a claim ticket until I see it.
I've seen it, but I don't read it. Far too violent. I prefer my hometown newspaper.
The Newark Bee. An excellent paper--much better than most.
I'm not the best person to ask about that.
Yvette and I have an arrangement. I clean her laundry free of charge.
I am not one to kiss and tell. Let us leave it at that, shall we?
No, indeed. I have no wish to spoil a good thing.
Ziggy? No one by that name has come in. I would remember it. Rather a good name for a comic strip, though.
It's a baseball, and a finely preserved one. Good heavens--that is Babe Ruth's signature. Rather valuable, I should think.
Do I look like a baseball player? I haven't played since high school. A .270 average--not bad for a ninety-eight-pound weakling.
This claim ticket is two years old today. You're a very fortunate woman; I was about to give the garment away.
It will be ready Tuesday. I'm joking, of course--an old laundryman's favourite.
You worry unnecessarily. No one returns for laundry after two years.
The lady who owned this dress is probably dead by now. A sobering thought.
No, thank you. I don't care for corned beef. I prefer more traditional Chinese cooking.
Please. I don't wish to offend, but kindly keep your hands to yourself.
Please don't touch me. My wife is a very jealous woman, and I permit no hanky-panky in the shop.
I'm sorry, but the dress is no longer my problem. Give it away if you like.
What are you looking at?
Let me know if you find anything. I do enjoy a good mystery.
Hmm. Those ink stains are quite dreadful. They will never come clean; you would be better off buying a new notebook.
Ah, yes. This certificate is good for one free pressing. Keep it; you may need my services someday.
No, thank you. I'm not hungry, particularly not for corned beef. I've had quite enough starch today.
This is not a clothing shop, madam. I cannot sell unclaimed garments. Imagine how cross the owners would be.
After two years, unclaimed laundry goes to the Salvation Army.
Join the Salvation Army and perhaps they'll give you something suitable.
Back again? I'm starting to think you have a crush on me. I'm a busy man--what can I do for you?
Ticket, please. You're here to pick something up?
Very well, look as long as you like. Looking is free; laundry is not.
The framed Chinese calligraphy lends the shop a dignified air.
You suspect Lo Fat enjoys watching customers pretend they can read it.
An ornate Chinese dragon decorates the counter. Your journalism courses at Tulane did not prepare you to interpret its symbolism.
As Lo Fat would probably tell you, stealing the shop's lantern is a poor way to brighten your prospects.
You attempt to converse with the lantern. It remains silent, though Lo Fat appears quietly amused.
A small smile flickers across Lo Fat's usually composed features.
An older Chinese American gentleman stands behind the counter, hard at work with an industrial iron.
